headline: Scientists Built an AI Robot Lab That Ran 11,382 DNA Steps Alone
author: Nexus Futura
text:
Scientists Built an AI Robot Lab That Ran 11,382 DNA Steps Alone

In a landmark November 2026 study published in Nature (DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11228-6, PMID: 42983087), researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) led by Mingyu Wu, Zhaoguo Wang, Chunhai Fan, Fei Wang, and Haibo Chen unveiled AutoDNA, an AI-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory capable of orchestrating more than 20 types of laboratory instruments across over 11,382 hardware operations. Highlighted on the cover of Nature News by Heidi Ledford (DOI: 10.1038/d41586-026-03552-8) and analyzed in a Nature News and Views commentary by Stanford University Professor James Zou (DOI: 10.1038/d41586-026-03270-1), the platform executes complex nucleic acid synthesis, transcription, polymerase chain reaction amplification, and sequencing workflows from a single natural-language prompt.

While artificial intelligence models can design candidate proteins and genetic sequences in minutes, validating those designs in a physical wet lab typically takes weeks or months of manual pipetting. Existing automated setups rely on rigid, task-specific scripts that struggle to coordinate diverse instruments. AutoDNA overcomes this bottleneck through a multi-agent operating system built on OpenHarmony that co-designs language-model reasoning, protocol generation, and real-time robotic scheduling. Across four benchmark demonstrations, AutoDNA optimized enzymatic DNA synthesis to a 97.8 percent yield, accelerated concurrent experimental protocols by 3.2-fold, completed a 203.5-hour end-to-end DNA digital data storage cycle across 78 DNA strands with 100 percent data recovery, and autonomously identified and validated a clinical KRAS G13D colorectal cancer mutation across 9,551 hardware steps.

By reducing human involvement to routine hardware maintenance and reagent replenishment, AutoDNA establishes a practical blueprint for science-as-a-service in synthetic biology, medical diagnostics, and molecular information storage. Researchers also emphasize strict biosafety guardrails, human authorization checkpoints, and real-time monitoring before extending autonomous laboratories to living organisms.
